column3: AI is everywhere. It unlocks your phone, picks your next song, and answers your questions.
But how does a computer actually learn? Let's find out.
This is Sam. And this is Bit: a brand-new computer that knows... absolutely nothing. Sam wants to teach Bit one simple thing: how to spot a cat.
The old way is to write rules. Pointy ears. Fur. A long, fluffy tail. Easy!
Until someone else walks in.
The real world is way too messy for rules. So, let's try something completely different.
Instead of rules, we show Bit examples. Lots of them. A picture, and the right answer. Cat. Dog. Cat. Cat. Dog.
At first, Bit just guesses.
Every time it's wrong, it turns its tiny dials, just a little, so next time it's a bit less wrong.
Then again. And again. A million times.
This time, nobody told Bit what a cat looks like. It found the pattern by itself. That's called machine learning.
Well... it only knows what it's been shown.
So what's inside Bit? Not a tiny brain. Just numbers.
A picture goes in as numbers. They flow through layers of tiny switches, and each dial sets how strongly one switch listens to the next.
Learning just means finding the right setting for every dial. Today's biggest AIs have billions of them.
Chatbots learn the same way, but with words. They read a gigantic library: more text than you could read in thousands of lifetimes.
And they practise one game, over and over: guess the next word.
Play that game well enough, and you can write a whole answer, one word at a time.
But here's the catch. A chatbot guesses what sounds right, not what's true.
So treat AI like a clever friend who's sometimes confidently wrong. Ask good questions. Check the answers. And keep your own brain switched on.
